# Session 14: Error Analysis & Report

## 📋 Agenda

- **Error analysis** — the highest-value part of the project
- Writing your own two-page report from the numbers on screen
- Building the bundle, and checking it reproduces
- Five slides

## 🎯 Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

- Attribute concrete errors to the **model** or to the **scheme**, with a reason.
- Write limitations specific to your run.
- Assemble a submission bundle and verify the notebook runs on a fresh runtime.

# Error analysis

## Two different findings in one table

```{.python}
errors = show_errors(test, pred_final)     # the held-out half, from the frozen file
```

Four different findings live in that one table, and sorting them is the analysis:

| | |
|---|---|
| **`model`** | the label is clear, both coders agreed at once, and the model still missed it |
| **`scheme`** | the item is genuinely borderline *under your scheme* |
| **`wording`** | the label *name* misleads — this one your next prompt could fix |
| **`ambiguous`** | the item is unclear in a way no scheme would settle |

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## `scheme` and `wording` are the pair to be careful about
One is fixable by prompting and the other is not. Confusing them is how a group spends three rounds on a problem no prompt can reach.
:::

## Overlap is a finding

```{.python}
overlap = errors_on_disagreed(errors, disagreed)   # disagreed: saved by 03
```

You already know which items are borderline, because you argued about them in Session 12. If the model's errors cluster there, that is a result:

> *"The model's B1/B2 confusions fall almost entirely on the 12 items our annotators also disagreed on. We read this as a property of the scheme's boundary rather than a failure of the model."*

. . .

A sentence like this is worth more in your report than the F1 value itself.

## Be concrete

::: {.callout-warning}
## Weak
"The model struggled with C1."
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Strong
"id 6 — *'Pseudogenes are generally thought of as the last stage…'* — gold C1, predicted C2. The sentence is syntactically simple but lexically dense; our scheme weights syntax, and the model appears to weight vocabulary. **A scheme problem**: our own coders disagreed on this item."
:::

# The report

## The notebook prints; you write

Nothing drafts the report for you. Every number it needs is on screen in `06_report.ipynb`:

| Section | Where the numbers are |
|---|---|
| 2 Methodology | your κ and counts, from notebook 03 |
| 3 Prompt iterations | the rounds-and-reasons table, step 1 |
| 4 Evaluation | per-class P/R/F1 and the matrix, step 3 |
| 5 Error analysis | `show_errors`, step 4 |

Two pages, six sections, in Word. **One per person** — the study is the group's, the report is yours.

## Limitations that are actually yours

::: {.callout-warning}
## Generic — true of every project on the course
"LLM output is stochastic." · "Contamination risk." · "Small sample."
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Yours
"Our C2 class has only 7 items because the pool contains 33 in total, so per-class C2 scores are effectively anecdotal." · "We adjudicated 12 of 42 items, so our gold reflects two coders' reading of an ambiguous boundary, not a settled one."
:::

# Handing in

## One command

```bash
python scripts/make_submission.py --group groupA
```

**Keeps** the folder structure — `scripts/ · prompts/ · data/ · outputs/` — because that layout follows the S10 checklist, and because the notebook's `../` paths require it.

**Leaves out**: `.git/`, `.venv/`, **your `.env`**, the large pool files, and anything from ICNALE.

**Reports** anything that is missing.

## Then check it reproduces

::: {.callout-important}
## Restart the runtime and Run all
If your notebook only runs in the session where you built it cell by cell, **it does not reproduce**, and reproducibility is what you are claiming.
:::

. . .

The bundle is self-contained for the claim you are making: given your gold set and your frozen predictions, anyone can recompute your numbers with **no API key and no network access**.

## Five slides

One per report section:

1. Scheme & gold
2. Prompt iterations
3. Evaluation
4. Error analysis
5. Limitations

**Every group member speaks.** Have your `show_errors` table open before you start.
